A 35-year-old woman comes to the clinic with complaints of low back pain that has persisted for 4
weeks. The pain worsens with forward bending and has not been adequately relieved by non-steroidal

anti-inflammatory medications. She reports giving birth one month ago but denies any other symptoms.
On physical examination, the sacral bases are found to be deep bilaterally, and the inferior lateral
angles are posterior on both sides. Her range of motion in the back is limited due to pain, but the
remainder of the examination is unremarkable. Which additional physical exam findings are most likely
in this patient? Answer Choices: (A) Positive spring test with sacral sulcus asymmetry on the left (B)
Positive spring test and negative seated flexion test (C) Negative spring test and equivocal seated
flexion test (D) Positive spring test and equivocal seated flexion test (E) Positive spring test and
positive seated flexion test on the right (F) Positive spring test with bilateral sacral sulcus asymmetry
(G) Positive spring test and positive seated flexion test on the left (H) Negative spring test and positive
seated flexion test on the left (I) Bilaterally positive seated flexion test with a negative spring test (J)
Positive spring test and positive sphinx test
 A. Positive spring test and positive sphinx test
B. Positive spring test and equivocal seated flexion test
C. Negative spring test and equivocal seated flexion test
D. Positive spring test and positive seated flexion test on the right
E. Bilaterally positive seated flexion test with a negative spring test
F. Positive spring test with sacral sulcus asymmetry on the left
G. Positive spring test with bilateral sacral sulcus asymmetry
H. Negative spring test and positive seated flexion test on the left
I. Positive spring test and positive seated flexion test on the left
J. Positive spring test and negative seated flexion test
